messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 59
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Violence: Violence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amal Haddad has worn a police uniform for thirty-five years, and for thirty-five years, it has felt like a second skin. Now, at fifty-nine, the crisp blue fabric feels like a costume she is no longer qualified to wear. It has been six months since the assault, and the woman who once commanded respect with a quiet word now spends her days in a state of high alert, monitoring not only the streets but the chaotic landscape of her own mind. The incident itself replays with pristine, terrifying clarity. It was a routine traffic stop on a rain-slicked Tuesday night, her partner at the wheel. Amal was in the passenger seat, running the plates, when the driver’s side door flew open and a man lunged not at her partner, but across the console, straight for her. The memory isn’t a story she tells herself; it’s a sensory immersion. She can still feel the suffocating pressure of his body, see the wild desperation in his eyes, and most of all, she hears the sound of his ragged breathing mixed with her own choked gasp, an auditory loop that starts without warning. Remembering it brings back the same paralyzing terror, a cold wave that starts in her stomach and leaves her breathless, convinced she is about to die all over again.

This feeling of imminent danger has bled out from the memory and contaminated her daily life. Amal has come to believe her own body is an enemy combatant. Any time her heart rate increases—climbing the stairs at the precinct, a brisk walk with her husband, a moment of exertion during a training drill—the pounding in her chest is no longer just a physiological response. It is the overture to the attack. Her mind immediately signals a catastrophic threat, and she is back in the passenger seat, trapped and helpless. This has made her work, a profession defined by moments of high adrenaline, feel like a minefield. She finds herself hesitating on calls involving any potential for violence, her focus split between the scene in front of her and the internal battle to keep her own panic from taking over.

The world outside her home now seems sorted into two categories: threats and potential threats. She is constantly scanning faces in a crowd, assessing gaits, watching hands, a professional instinct now dialed up to an unbearable, exhausting frequency. This hypervigilance extends to her own thoughts. She finds herself policing her own mind, constantly checking for signs that she is “losing it.” The fear that she is becoming unstable, unfit for duty, is a constant, nagging whisper. This internal surveillance is isolating, but it feels necessary. To manage the overwhelming sense of threat, Amal has systematically dismantled her own support system. The belief that she cannot truly rely on anyone has taken root and grown into a thorny barrier. Her partner was right there, after all, and he couldn't stop it. So how could anyone else? She no longer goes to weekly family dinners, offering vague excuses to her children. She lets calls from her oldest friends go to voicemail. Her husband, Samir, finds her sitting in silence in the evenings, the television off, and his attempts to connect are met with a wall of monosyllabic replies. It’s easier to be alone, she tells herself, than to pretend to be the person she was before.

The injustice of it all is a bitter pill she swallows every morning. The assailant was never caught. There was no resolution, no moment of reckoning. It was just a random act of violence that shattered her sense of safety and left her to pick up the pieces. This feeling of profound unfairness fuels a quiet, simmering anger that has nowhere to go. She feels abandoned by the system she has dedicated her life to. The final straw came last week, during a routine patrol. Her new partner was driving, and as they sat at a red light, a car full of teenagers pulled up alongside them, music blaring. For a split second, the feeling of being a passenger, of being trapped with activity just outside her window, was so overwhelming that she reached for her sidearm. Her partner’s quick, questioning glance was all it took for her to see how far she had fallen. Amal is here now because she is terrified of losing the last piece of her identity she has left: her badge. More than that, she is exhausted from the fight and quietly hopes, without much conviction, that it is still possible to feel safe in her own body again.
